summary: Defines an experimental MIB for managing Multicast Source Discovery Protocol speakers, described in RFC 3618. It is an experimental protocol document.

plainLanguage.summary: This lists the gauges you can read from a router running MSDP so you can see how it is doing.

subtitle: An experimental SNMP MIB that lets operators monitor and configure routers speaking the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol.

tldr.problem: Routers running the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) had no standard way to be monitored or configured through network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines MSDP-MIB, a MIB module with four scalars and four tables (one deprecated) covering peers, the Source-Active cache and mesh groups, placed under an experimental OID.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document that keeps an odd object layout on purpose, because existing implementations already used it. Several objects are deprecated since the features were removed from MSDP.

today: RFC 4624 is an Experimental document and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes management of MSDP, which RFC 3618 specifies.

sections.title: Introduction and Management Framework
sections.content:
RFC 4624 defines an experimental portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) speakers. MSDP itself is described in RFC 3618.

MIB objects are read and written through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The objects are written in SMIv2, defined in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. The wider Internet-Standard Management Framework is summarised in RFC 3410.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that runs MSDP is like a machine with a control panel. This document describes the panel so that a manager's program can read the gauges and turn some knobs.

sections.title: What the MIB Contains
sections.content:
The module holds four scalars and four tables, one of them deprecated:

  • Requests Table (deprecated): the longest-match table used to pick the peer for SA-Requests for a group. It is deprecated because Requests were removed from MSDP before it became an RFC.
  • Peer Table: information about the system's peers.
  • Source-Active (SA) Cache Table: the SA cache entries.
  • Mesh Group Table: the MSDP mesh groups this system belongs to.

The module uses the IpAddress syntax, so it only suits IPv4 systems. The RFC explains that MSDP itself is IPv4-only and the working group made an explicit decision not to create an IPv6 version of the protocol.

The module is admittedly disorganised: scalars before and after tables, holes in the OID space, and RowStatus in the middle of tables. Objects were added and removed as MSDP evolved, and renumbering was planned for a move to the standard mib-2 tree. When the working group published MSDP as Experimental, it kept the experimental OID and the existing order instead, because implementations already used it.
sections.plainLanguage: The panel has a few single gauges and four lists: one old list nobody uses any more, one for neighbours, one for remembered announcements, and one for friend groups. It looks messy because it was built bit by bit and people already depended on it.

sections.title: Peers, Cache and Mesh Groups
sections.content:
The scalars include msdpEnabled (MSDP globally on or off), msdpCacheLifetime (the lifetime given to SA cache entries, where 0 means no SA caching), msdpNumSACacheEntries and msdpRPAddress (the Rendezvous Point address used when sourcing SA messages, possibly 0.0.0.0 on non-RPs).

The Peer Table is indexed by the remote peer address. It reports the connection state (inactive, listen, connecting, established or disabled), counters for SA messages, control messages and encapsulated data packets in each direction, the number of Peer-RPF failures, and timestamps such as when the peer last entered or left the ESTABLISHED state. Writable settings include the local address, connect-retry interval, hold time, keepalive period, the minimum TTL for SA encapsulation and the encapsulation type (none or tcp). Rows are added or removed with msdpPeerStatus, which triggers the MSDP 'Enable MSDP peering' and 'Disable MSDP peering' events. Several counters carry a discontinuity timestamp, msdpPeerDiscontinuityTime.

Defaults are given by the module: connect retry 30 seconds, hold time 75 seconds, keepalive 60 seconds, data TTL 1, and TCP port 639 for both ends. Notification and SA-Response objects are deprecated because they were removed from the MSDP specification.

The SA Cache Table is indexed by group address, source address and originating RP. The RP is in the index to help diagnose incorrect advertisements. Rows cannot be created through SNMP, only deleted. Each row shows the time remaining before it expires. The Mesh Group Table is indexed by mesh group name and peer address.
sections.plainLanguage: For each neighbour router the panel shows if the line is up, how many messages went each way, and a few settings. It also lists the announcements the router remembers, each with a countdown until it is forgotten, and the named groups of routers that all talk to each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access can be dangerous if set by the wrong party. The RFC walks through examples:

  • Changing msdpEnabled can simply disable MSDP processing on the router.
  • Setting msdpCacheLifetime below a peer's refresh interval makes all state time out and be refreshed.
  • Changing msdpRPAddress can break the Peer-RPF rules for SA messages the router sources.
  • msdpSACacheStatus can remove valid entries from the SA cache.
  • Wrong mesh group settings can cause subtle protocol misbehaviour.

Reading is sensitive too: the Peer Table and Mesh Group Table can reveal internal topology, and the SA cache can reveal active private sources and groups. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC says it is RECOMMENDED to use SNMPv3 with its cryptographic mechanisms, and deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. The operator remains responsible for giving access only to legitimate principals.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can turn the knobs could switch the router off or confuse it, and even just looking at the gauges could reveal secrets about the network. So only trusted people should get access, using the secure version of SNMP.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: Because this MIB is for an experimental protocol, it lives under the experimental part of the OID tree. The module is registered as MSDP-MIB with number 92 and the description 'Multicast Source Discovery MIB'.
sections.plainLanguage: The panel gets its own official label number, 92, in the part of the tree set aside for experiments.
